prerequisites: Basic knowledge of Physics 1 and Mathematical Analysis: vector calculus, integral and differential calculus, linear algebra, forces and moments

learning_outcomes.text: Acquiring knowledge of the theoretical foundations of the mechanical behavior of materials for structural use and their experimental characterization under simple loading conditions.
Acquiring fundamental knowledge of the procedures for predicting the stress state, deformability, and strength of one-dimensional mechanical parts subjected to static loads.
The student will acquire the necessary knowledge to identify and analyze the relationships between the material's constitutive properties and the structural behavior of the mechanical component.
The student will acquire the ability to analyze the deformation and stress states of structural elements to predict strength.
The student will acquire the ability to identify procedures for characterizing the mechanical response of materials, identifying the most significant properties for selecting materials for use.
The student will gain the ability to assess the deformability and strength properties of mechanical components for a given structural application.

Acquiring the ability to communicate with both specialists and non-specialists about the requirements and performance associated with specific mechanical properties of structural materials, explaining the experimental methodologies required for their characterization, and discussing possible design approaches for their use in structural components.

The student will be able to address original and innovative aspects related to the characterization, selection, and use of materials for the design, verification, and realization of structural components subjected to static loads with a high degree of autonomy.

syllabus_topics: Kinematic analysis of the rigid body
Analysis of isostatic structures: support reactions and calculation of internal actions
Characteristics of stresses and De Saint Venant's cases: beams subjected to normal, bending, shear, and torsional forces; representation of stress states (Mohr's circles)
The mechanical properties of materials, mechanical tests for tension, compression, bending, and impact
Principle of Virtual Work: calculation of displacements and hyperstatic structures
Design and verification of mechanical components: Strength criteria (maximum normal stress, maximum shear stress, maximum distortion energy, Coulomb's criterion)
teaching_methods: Lectures with numerical examples and exercises

assessment_methods.method: Written test - Theoretical questions with open-ended answers

assessment_rules: The final exam consists of a written test with two parts: exercises (maximum 21 points) and theoretical questions (maximum 10 points), for a total maximum score of 30. To pass, a total score greater than or equal to 18 is required, along with a passing grade in both parts. Specifically, at least 12 points are needed in the exercises and at least 5.5 points in the theory section. Submission and approval of the written report for laboratory topics are necessary conditions for registration for the exam. No oral examination is foreseen.
